column2: What will happen if you apply @Target(ElementType.TYPE) to an annotation and try to use it on a method parameter?
column8: @Target(ElementType.TYPE) restricts the annotation to types only. Using it on method parameters will cause a compilation error.

column2: Which @Retention policy allows annotations to be processed by annotation processors at compile time but not retained in class files?
column8: SOURCE retention allows compile-time processing but annotations are discarded after compilation.

column2: What is the purpose of the @interface keyword when creating custom annotations?
column8: @interface is used to declare annotation types in Java, not regular interfaces.

column2: If you create an annotation with @Retention(RetentionPolicy.CLASS) and try to access it via reflection at runtime, what happens?
column8: CLASS retention means annotations are in class files but not available at runtime via reflection.

column2: Which combination of @Target values allows an annotation to be used on both fields and methods?
column8: Use array syntax with curly braces to specify multiple target types.

column2: What happens when you don't specify @Retention on a custom annotation?
column8: When @Retention is not specified, it defaults to RetentionPolicy.CLASS.

column2: In a custom validation annotation, which @Target and @Retention combination is most appropriate for runtime field validation?
column8: Runtime field validation requires RUNTIME retention and FIELD target to access field annotations at runtime.
